The objective and secondary objectives are the course's own titles. Their values (report a temperature above 100.4 F (38 C); check the fundus, bladder and lochia; a boggy uterus displaced above the umbilicus and to one side often means a full bladder, so help the client empty it and massage the fundus; postpartum hemorrhage is 1,000 mL or more within 24 hours) are the course seed's reading of OpenStax Maternal-Newborn Nursing (2024) sections 20.1, 20.3 and 21.2 (PDF read 2026-10-31 and 2026-11-02).

brief.situation: 04:00 on a postpartum unit. You are the LPN caring for four stable postpartum clients with an RN. Ms. Alvarez, 29, had a vaginal birth at 22:00 after a long labor; birth loss was 350 mL. You wake her for her 04:00 check. She says she feels 'wet' and a bit crampy.
handover: Second baby; epidural removed at 23:30. Oxytocin infusion finished at 00:00. Up once with help at 01:00; has not voided since the birth.
Order set: straight catheter if unable to void within 6 hours of birth; vital signs every 4 hours; call the RN with any change.
Unit practice: weigh pads to measure blood loss (1 g is 1 mL). Your phone reaches the RN at once.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Medicines for bleeding are the RN's and the provider's; your part is to find it, act within your scope and report it so it lands.
Partway through you are asked to write what is happening and why. A debrief scores what you did.

parts.label: Recognition
parts.criteria: Names uterine atony with heavy bleeding (boggy fundus, soaked pads), caused or worsened by a full bladder (fundus high and pushed to one side, not voided in 6 hours); knows that 1,000 mL is postpartum hemorrhage and that vital signs can stay normal until late; the temperature of 100.0 F is not a fever to report.
parts.modelAnswer: Her uterus is boggy and she is bleeding heavily. It sits high and off to the right because her bladder is full: she hasn't voided since the birth. If the loss reaches 1,000 mL it is a hemorrhage, and her pulse and pressure may look fine until late. 100.0 F is not a fever.

parts.label: Actions and scope
parts.criteria: Massage the fundus at once; empty the bladder without walking her (bedpan or the standing-order catheter); weigh the pads; phone the RN with numbers and stay with her; vital signs; the RN gives the uterotonic; document.
parts.modelAnswer: Massage the fundus until firm, phone the RN from the room with the findings and numbers, empty her bladder on a bedpan or with the catheter rather than walking her, weigh the pads and take her vital signs. The oxytocin is the RN's. Then document.

expertPath.text: Fundus: boggy, high and to the right. Massage until firm. Look at the pad: soaked.
Phone the RN from the bedside: boggy fundus, deviated, no void in 6 hours, soaked pads, vital signs. Come now.
Bedpan or the standing-order catheter, not a walk. Weigh the pads. Vital signs: 100.0 F is not a fever.

fall.headline: She fainted and fell
fall.body: After a heavy loss, standing can drop her blood pressure. Empty the bladder in bed: bedpan or the catheter order.

shock.headline: Hemorrhagic shock
shock.body: A boggy uterus with soaked pads needs massage, an empty bladder and a clear report at once. Vital signs can look normal until late.

controlled.headline: Found, reported and controlled
controlled.body: You massaged the fundus, emptied her bladder safely, measured the loss and got the RN there with numbers. That is the expert path.

controlledLate.headline: Controlled, by a slower or riskier route
controlledLate.body: Look at when you massaged, how and when her bladder was emptied, and how the RN was reached.

time_up.headline: Never reported
time_up.body: Heavy postpartum bleeding is reported to the RN at once, even when your own measures are working.

scoring.modelReasoning: A boggy fundus above the umbilicus and pushed to one side, with soaked pads in a woman who has not voided for 6 hours, is uterine atony worsened by a full bladder. Massage the fundus until firm while supporting the lower uterus, and empty the bladder in bed (a bedpan, or the standing-order catheter), not by walking her, because a heavy loss can make her faint. Phone the RN from the bedside with the findings and the numbers; weighing the pads turns 'a lot of blood' into milliliters, and 1,000 mL is a hemorrhage. Her pulse and pressure may stay normal until late. The uterotonic is the RN's, by the provider's order. A temperature of 100.0 F in the first day is not a fever to report. Document it all.
